headlines.title: No longer a secret, Nathan Fielder's Elizabeth Holmes doc ‘You Can See Everything' lands in New York
headlines.description: No longer a secret, “You Can See Everything,” Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s Elizabeth Holmes documentary, premiered Wednesday at the New York Film Festival. Since first debuting in a surprise, no-phones screening at the Telluride Film Festival on Sept. 6, “You Can See Everything” immediately transformed into one of the year’s most buzzed-about films. Shot secretly over three years, the nearly three-hour documentary captures Holmes, founder of the medical testing company Theranos, in the 34 days before reporting to prison. But as fans of Fielder would expect, little in how “You Can See Everything” follows a conventional route. Moviegoers lined up outside the Alice Tully Hall at Lincoln Center as early as 3 a.m. in hopes of attending the sold-out 8 p.m. screening. “You Can See Everything,” which A24 will release Oct. 16, is a hard-to-believe coda to a preposterous saga. Even Fielder isn’t sure what to make of the surreal odyssey he and Oppenheim captured. “I am still struggling to this day to understand what I went through,” Fielder said in a Q&A following the screening. Crime and Courts Sep 24 Movies Sep 7 After her conviction on four felony counts of fraud and conspiracy, Holmes entered a Texas prison in May 2023. In a headline-grabbing scandal that rocked Silicon Valley, one of the most surprising and surreal twists was revealed only this month. Holmes chose to let Fielder, the absurdist comedian of “Nathan For You” and “The Rehearsal,” and the documentary filmmaker Oppenheim, intimately film her life with her partner, the California hotel heir Billy Evans, and their two children. At this dramatic moment in their lives, Fielder lived in a guest house at their Del Mar, California, beachside home. The filmmakers shot from morning to night. Fielder interviews the couple while in bed, or the bathroom. “I mean, I cannot tell you how weird it was that we were there,” Fielder said. “I wouldn’t think I’d be, like, the person that you would want for your final 34 days of freedom. I’m not the most, like, comforting.” The filmmakers happened to hear that Holmes and Evans had reached out to A24 about the prospect of making a documentary. Fielder didn’t initially think it would amount to a feature film, but he was curious just to meet Holmes. “When I met her, I remember having this weird experience,” Fielder explained. “She seems so genuine at times but then I’m like, (expletive), tracking my thoughts and being like, ‘I know she’s a liar.’” “Every person who worked on this movie was going through a similar cognitive dissonance,” said Oppenheim, who directed the just-released “Primetime,” starring Robert Pattinson as “To Catch a Predator” host Chris Hansen. “We would unpack the day’s events and no one could agree on seemingly mundane moments that would transpire.” In “You Can See Everything,” Fielder seeks not only to grasp what is true and not true about Holmes, but to grapple with deeper questions of identity, performance, fiction and control. Holmes founded Theranos with her then-romantic partner Ramesh “Sunny” Balwani. They promised the company would revolutionize healthcare with a technology that could quickly scan for diseases and other health problems with a few drops of blood taken with a finger prick. The hype helped them raise nearly $1 billion from investors. By 2014, Theranos was valued at $4.5 billion. But after the company’s purported technology advances were exposed in a series of explosive articles in The Wall Street Journal, the company collapsed. In 2018, the U.S. Justice Department charged Holmes and Balwani with a litany of white-collar crimes. Balwani was separately convicted in 12 felony counts of fraud and conspiracy and sentenced to nearly 13 years in a Southern California prison. The filmmakers more than once asked the Alice Tully Hall crowd to preserve the surprise twists and turns the movie takes as it shifts. That includes dramatic recreations with the aid of an A-list star and other elaborations, all in an effort to get closer to the truth. But even as Fielder and Oppenheimer pleaded for viewers not to discuss the film in too much detail, they were clearly eager to debate and try to make sense of “You Can See Everything.” “As each scene that happens, it’s happening and we’re documenting it. There’s no plan of what’s going to happen next at any point,” Fielder said. “This is a path that opened up to us and we just followed it.”

headlines.title: Oakland's Skyline High cancels remainder of varsity football season
headlines.description: Oakland’s Skyline High School is reportedly canceling the remainder of its varsity football season because of a lack of players and safety concerns. According to the East Bay Times, the school’s principal sent an email indicating the team does not have the required number of players because of injuries, transfers and other issues. The shortage led to safety concerns and prompted the decision to cancel the remainder of the season. Skyline had already forfeited its previous three games for the same reasons. Other Bay Area high schools have made similar moves this fall, including Richmond and Mount Diablo.

headlines.title: SF lifts shelter-in-place, evacuations after underground vault eruptions
headlines.description: A shelter-in-place order and evacuations were lifted Thursday after four underground vaults erupted in downtown San Francisco, according to the San Francisco Fire Department. Firefighters responded around 6:04 a.m. to the 100 to 200 block of California Street following reports of smoke coming from several street-side underground vaults. Four vaults experienced eruptions that were isolated to the vaults, SFFD said. A unified command was established with the San Francisco Police Department, SFFD and PG&E. The immediate area was evacuated and the surrounded area also was cordoned off. There were shelter-in-place orders in the 100 to 300 blocks of California and Front streets until around 10 a.m. PG&E shut down additional power, which affected more locations in the area. Power has since been restored to all but one affected customers, the utility said. No injuries have been reported. The San Francisco Fire Department and PG&E are investigating the cause of the fire.

headlines.title: 3 indicted in kidnapping, killing of Tracy man
headlines.description: Three people who remain at large have been indicted in connection with the February kidnapping and killing of a Tracy man who investigators determined was not the intended target, the San Joaquin County Sheriff’s Office said. Avtar Singh, 57, was kidnapped Feb. 17 from the Gurdwara Gur Nanak Parkash in Tracy. Surveillance video showed a white SUV and three people dressed in dark clothing apparently forcing Singh into the vehicle. Singh’s body was found days later in a remote area near Lake Berryessa. The Napa County Sheriff’s Office located his body on Feb. 20. Singh was survived by his wife and 6-month-old triplets. Investigators later determined that he was not the intended target, the San Joaquin County Sheriff’s Office said in a statement Wednesday. The people indicted are Alberto Alonso Alencastro, 25; Alfonso Cresencio Segura Arellano, 20; and Barnabe Antonio Segura Arellano, 22. (L-R) Alberto Alencastro, Alfonso Segura, and Barnabe Segura. (San Joaquin County Sheriff’s Office) All three remain at large. Authorities are asking anyone who recognizes them, knows their whereabouts, or has information that could help investigators to contact the San Joaquin County Sheriff’s Office. Authorities warned people not to approach or try to apprehend the three.

headlines.title: Former airline pilot, girlfriend convicted of child sex abuse, East Bay DA says
headlines.description: A former airline pilot and his girlfriend were convicted of child sexual abuse, the Contra Costa County District Attorney’s Office said Wednesday. Florida resident Rustom Bhagwagar, 35, a former pilot for Delta Airlines, was arrested at the San Francisco International Airport in July 2025 by the Contra Costa County Sheriff’s Office and was held on $15 million bail. He was charged with 24 felonies related to the repeated sex abuse of a young girl. The criminal case against Bhagwagar and co-defendant and Walnut Creek resident Jennifer Spitz Powell, 46, was handled by two separate juries, prosecutors said. A jury found Powell guilty on Monday, and another jury found Bhagwagar guilty on Tuesday. Both were convicted of eight counts of sex abuse on a child under 10 years of age and 12 counts of forcible lewd acts upon a child under the age of 14. Evidence presented to both juries showed that the sexual abuse of the victim began when she was 7 years old and occurred from 2017 to 2022. Powell, who was in a relationship with Bhagwagar, participated with him in numerous acts of abuse against the victim, according to prosecutors. Bhagwagar and Powell each face a maximum sentence of 230 years to life in state prison and will be sentenced at a future date, the district attorney’s office said. “This young survivor showed extraordinary courage by testifying in court and facing the people who used duress to harm her,” said District Attorney Diana Becton in a statement released by her office. “These verdicts hold both defendants accountable.”
headlines.source: Katy St. Clair | Bay City News

headlines.title: Valkyries fans remain optimistic heading into playoff game 3 against Dallas
headlines.description: Fans of the Golden State Valkyries said they remain optimistic — despite the team’s loss in game 2 of the first round of the WNBA playoffs to the Dallas Wings — that their team will prevail in this postseason run. While the Valkyries were in Dallas Wednesday playing at the home of the Wings, Bay Area fans headed to watch parties locally to tune in to the game. Likely the largest watch party was the official, free watch party on the big screen at Thrive City just outside Chase Center. This time, Valkyries fans added a new tradition. Borrowing from the success of pre-watch party marches up to Thrive City during World Cup matches, Valkyries fans marched by the hundreds up the block ahead of Wednesday’s game. They were led by the Valkyries’ mascot, Violet, and Oakland’s Fremont High School marching band. Fans stayed in Thrive City watching the game as it stretched into overtime, cycling back between elation and disappointment as the teams traded off taking the lead in the game. Ultimately, the Wings bested the Valkyries 108 to 100. With the series now tied at 1-1, the teams will next face off on Friday, October 2, at the Valkyries home at Chase Center. Valkyries fans on Wednesday said they are feeling optimistic that the Valkyries will have a home-court advantage with the fan energy at Ballhalla on Friday. Many fans said they believe the Valkyries could make it all the way this year in the playoffs. “I’m feeling pretty confident that they’re going to pull it off, hopefully they’ll go to the very end and win,” said Judy Bacchus of Hayward. The Valkyries are in their second season as a team and in their second postseason run. Fans said the energy and confidence this postseason feels particularly high. “It’s so wonderful that San Francisco got a women’s basketball team, and I think that we here in the Bay Area want to support that,” Bacchus said. “And the fans have proven that, coming out, selling out the arena every game, so I want to be a part of that,” she continued.

headlines.title: Ogunbowale scores WNBA playoff-record 45 as Wings win in OT to force deciding game with Valkyries
headlines.description: Arike Ogunbowale scored a WNBA playoff-record 45 points, including a tying 3-pointer in the final seconds of regulation, and the Dallas Wings beat the Golden State Valkyries 108-100 in an overtime thriller Wednesday night, forcing a deciding Game 3 in their first-round series. Ogunbowale opened the extra period by banking in a 3, then hit another one to put Dallas ahead for good at 103-100 with 1:46 remaining. She easily topped her previous playoff best of 24 points. The four-time All-Star’s off-balance corner 3 for a 93-93 tie with 4.1 seconds left in Game 2 was followed by Gabby Williams getting called for an offensive foul on the inbound play after a Golden State timeout. That call was reversed on replay, so instead of Aziaha James having a chance to give Dallas the lead at the free-throw line, there was a jump ball at center court with 3.0 seconds to go. After a scramble for the loose ball, Golden State’s desperation shot was way off target, and after the buzzer. The deciding game will be Friday night in San Francisco, where the Valkyries won the series opener by 24 points. Golden State is looking to advance in the playoffs for the first time in the franchise’s second season. The late drama overshadowed an off night for Wings star Paige Bueckers, who is making her postseason debut. The 2025 No. 1 overall pick and Rookie of the Year scored 10 points on 3-of-13 shooting. Williams scored a career-high 36 points, regular season or playoffs, but missed all six of her shots in the final 1:31 of overtime to finish 12 of 23 from the field. Dallas’ Alysha Clark tied her playoff career high with 21 points. ___ See AP’s full WNBA coverage here

headlines.title: Hilton, Becerra clash over homelessness, Trump in California gubernatorial debate
headlines.description: Republican Steve Hilton and Democrat Xavier Becerra clashed nonstop for an hour Wednesday in the sole televised debate in their contest for California governor, presenting sharply contrasting visions for how they would deal with homelessness, soaring household costs and high taxes in the nation’s most populous state. Hilton presented himself as a change agent, saying that years of Democratic dominance in Sacramento had diminished the state in business, education and quality of life. “We’ve got to try something different,” he said in the matchup on CNN. Becerra depicted Hilton as President Donald Trump’s handpicked choice for the job, and repeatedly invoked the president’s name throughout the debate. “You can hear Donald Trump” in Hilton’s responses, he said at one point. The debate played out just days before mail ballots are expected to begin arriving at homes in advance of the Nov. 3 general election. Looking to replace outgoing Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom, Hilton is appealing to voters who he says are desperate for change in a state known for its punishing cost of living, high taxes and long-running homeless crisis. Becerra is promising to bring down household costs, too, while continuing to push back against Trump’s agenda. A September poll conducted by the University of California, Berkeley, Institute of Governmental Studies found that Becerra had a sizable lead over Hilton. A Republican has not won a statewide election in heavily Democratic California since 2006. Hilton has been holding a steady string of public events to try to attract voters’ attention, while Becerra has run a lower-key campaign. He thanked CNN “for bringing Xavier out of hiding,” a dig at his rival as the debate got underway. Hilton has Trump’s endorsement, but that could be a liability at a time when the president’s popularity has been sliding while voters grouse over climbing gas and grocery prices. Trump has had a long-strained relationship with California, where he was trounced in his three runs for the White House. The two rivals emerged from a chaotic primary that saw former Democratic U.S. Rep. Eric Swalwell exit the race — then announce he would leave Congress — following allegations that he sexually assaulted a woman twice, including when she worked for him, while billionaire Tom Steyer ran the most expensive political advertising campaign in the country in a losing effort for the Democratic nomination. Hilton has vowed to bring down the price of gasoline to $3 a gallon, about half the current cost; cut in half residents’ utility bills, now among the nation’s highest; and eliminate state income taxes on the first $150,000 in earnings. Becerra has been leaning into his long resume in government as he maneuvers to take charge of the state. He spent more than 35 years in state and federal office, including leadership roles in the U.S. House, as California’s attorney general, and as former President Joe Biden’s health secretary. “The governor’s office is not a place with training wheels,” he likes to say.
headlines.source: Sophie Austin and Michael R. Blood - The Associated Press

headlines.title: Newsom vetoes measure that would have penalized the use of smart glasses to secretly record people
headlines.description: California Gov. Gavin Newsom vetoed legislation Wednesday that would have penalized Californians for using smart glasses to record people without their permission in changing rooms, doctor’s offices and other spaces people generally consider private. The legislation also would have required companies making smart glasses or other wearable devices, starting in 2028, to include a light or some other feature that indicates that the person is video or audio recording. It would have banned the sale of technology designed to help people conceal a recording light or sound on a smart device. Newsom wrote in a letter explaining his decision that the bill’s definition of a wearable recording device was too broad. He noted that the state already bars people from recording someone without their consent in spaces generally considered private. Meta Ray-Bans, smart glasses that were rolled out in 2021, have especially grown in popularity, with more than 7 million of the AI-powered devices being sold last year. State Sen. Eloise Gómez Reyes, who wrote the bill, said it would’ve helped the state respond to the technology’s rapid growth. “Whatever we can do to protect an individual’s right to privacy, we have to do,” she said. The bill would have been the first of its kind in the nation and built upon the state’s extensive privacy protections. California is one of about a dozen states that already requires both parties’ consent before a conversation can be recorded via audio or video. Reyes’ proposal was designed to clarify that it applied to smart glasses and make it easier for someone to tell when those devices are recording. Any person who violated the bill by secretly recording someone would have faced prison time or fines of up to $1,500. A company that made devices that didn’t comply with the bill would’ve faced fines up to $2,500. But TechNet, a group of executives from companies including Meta, Google and Amazon, said the legislation, known as SB 1130, would have been unfair to businesses and customers. “California already has extensive laws governing unlawful recording, and as currently written, SB 1130 is not the right approach to addressing these concerns,” TechNet Executive Director Robert Boykin said in a statement. Meta touted the benefits of its smart glasses in response to Newsom’s veto, including an initiative providing the devices to blinded veterans to help them read documents and identify objects. “We’re still in the early days of building this technology and we’re committed to continuing prioritizing privacy as we build,” a Meta spokesperson said in a statement. About a dozen states, including California, Massachusetts and Pennsylvania, require someone who wants to record a conversation to get the other person’s permission. It’s important to strengthen privacy laws for these wearable smart devices because it’s not as obvious to tell when a person is using them to record compared to when someone is filming with their phone or a camera, said Justin Brookman, the director of technology policy for Consumer Reports. In a letter to lawmakers earlier this year about the bill, Consumer Reports referenced a TikTok in which a woman recounted her experience getting a wax when she realized her technician was wearing smart glasses. The technician told the content creator, Aniessa Navarro, that the glasses weren’t on, but the experience was still unnerving, she said in the TikTok. The Consumer Reports letter cited a separate event in which a woman said she was secretly filmed with smart glasses at a gym and harassed online after the video was uploaded to social media. “The stories are enough to cause alarm, and we need to do something as soon as we can,” Reyes said at the end of the legislative session.

headlines.title: ‘Surveillance is not safety': Protesters push San Jose to shut down Flock camera network
headlines.description: Protesters on Wednesday issued a renewed call for San Jose to shut down its network of roughly 500 automated license plate reading cameras. The protesters rallied at City Hall before taking their complaints before a key City Council committee that’s trying to figure out the future of Flock cameras in San Jose. Supporters of the cameras argue they are invaluable public safety tools, while critics say they’re a dangerous invasion of privacy that are already being abused by law enforcement. Community groups represented in Wednesday’s protest have already filed a lawsuit against San Jose over the automated license plate readers (ALPRs). The protesters said a system that records so many people is a violation of privacy, adding the data can be abused to target groups or individuals. “Surveillance is not safety,” EFF Associate Director Rin Alajaji said. “That’s why EFF and the ACLU of Northern California are suing the city of San Jose on behalf of SIREN and CAIR, because in a single year San Jose PD ran over 250,000 warrantless searches on this location data.” Community anger recently intensified after NBC Bay Area reported a police officer had been fired after accessing ALPR data to help a family member involved in a domestic violence case. The gap between when the breach was discovered and when the officer was fired was more than a year. “None of this was disclosed to the council when it was reviewing the rules for ALPRs, including one of the rules being that there must be disclosure when an abuse occurs,” SIREN Executive Director Huy Tran said. The protesters took their complaints to the city’s rules committee, which was looking at two separate memos by councilmembers to revamp the ALPR system. “We definitely need to put provisions into place to create a system that is safer with more verifications, with opportunities to make our community feel safer and trust us again,” Vice Mayor Pam Foley said. The memos indicate officials would like to keep the cameras operating with more scrutiny, while protesters want them shut off. The committee told city staff to come back with a plan on how to approach revamping the system. Public hearings will then be held by the full council before any final decisions are made.

headlines.title: New California Poll: Economy, immigration drive voter concerns
headlines.description: A new NBCUniversal Local and Telemundo Station Group poll finds California likely voters are most concerned about affordability and the economy heading into the November election, while separate polling of Hispanic voters reveals notable differences on immigration, Gov. Gavin Newsom and housing policy. California voters are heading toward the November election with their wallets top of mind, according to the new polling that also finds strong concerns about homelessness, disapproval of President Donald Trump’s job performance and a complicated picture when it comes to immigration and enforcement. The statewide poll, conducted by Mason-Dixon Polling & Research, surveyed 625 registered California voters who said they were likely to vote in the November general election and has a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. A separate survey conducted over the same period questioned 400 Hispanic registered voters in California who also said they were likely to vote. That poll has a margin of error of plus or minus five percentage points. Margins of error are higher for regional, age, party and other subgroups. Both polls were conducted Sept. 21 through Sept. 24. Cost of living and the economy dominate voter concerns Cost of living and inflation ranked as the single most important issue for 25% of California likely voters, followed closely by the economy and jobs at 23%. Immigration and enforcement ranked third at 15%, followed by health care at 11% and foreign policy and the Iran war at 10%. Taken together, nearly half of voters selected either cost of living or the economy and jobs as their most important issue. Hispanic voters showed a similar focus on pocketbook concerns, though immigration ranked somewhat higher—29% chose cost of living and inflation, 22% selected the economy and jobs and 19% chose immigration and enforcement. Foreign policy and the Iran war, however, was the top concern for just 2% of Hispanic voters, compared with 10% statewide. The Economic Pressure The financial pressure voters describe is also reflected elsewhere in the survey. Statewide, 36% said their personal financial situation is worse than it was four years ago, compared with 22% who said it is better and 42% who said it is about the same. One in four California likely voters also said they are currently considering leaving the state because of the cost of living. Bay Area voters stood out in both questions. 27% of San Francisco/San Jose respondents said they were financially better off than four years ago — the highest percentage among the regions surveyed — while just 17% said they were considering leaving California because of the cost of living, the lowest regional figure. President Trump receives low marks; voters split on Gov. Newsom President Trump’s job performance received a negative assessment from California likely voters: 31% approved and 64% disapproved, with 5% unsure. Disapproval was highest in the Bay Area at 74%, while 21% approved. Voters were much more evenly divided on Governor Gavin Newsom. Statewide, 45% approved of the governor’s job performance and 46% disapproved. But Newsom performed better among Hispanic likely voters, with 54% approving and 38% disapproving — a nine-point difference in approval compared with voters statewide. Among Democrats surveyed statewide, 66% said they would be inclined to vote for Newsom if he sought the Democratic presidential nomination in 2028. That figure rose to 73% among Hispanic Democrats. The question was asked only of Democratic respondents and is not a measure of all California voters. The survey also asked voters about the choices for California’s next governor. Forty-nine percent said they were satisfied with Xavier Becerra and Steve Hilton as their two candidate choices, 25% were dissatisfied and 26% were unsure. Among Hispanic voters, 55% said they were satisfied. Immigration: A complicated picture Nearly two-thirds of California likely voters — 63% — described illegal immigration as either a very or somewhat serious problem for the state. But the same share, 63%, disapproved of how the federal government is enforcing immigration laws, compared with 30% who approved. And 53% of California voters said they support the state maintaining its sanctuary-state status, while 38% opposed it. Hispanic voters showed one of the clearest differences on that question: 68% supported California remaining a sanctuary state, 15 percentage points higher than the statewide electorate. At the same time, 62% of Hispanic voters said illegal immigration was a serious problem, while 66% disapproved of the federal government’s enforcement approach. The regional results also showed a pronounced Bay Area divide. Among all San Francisco/San Jose voters, 34% called illegal immigration a “very serious” problem, compared with 50% in Northern California and San Diego. Bay Area voters were also the most likely to disapprove of federal immigration enforcement, at 75%, and the most supportive of sanctuary-state status, at 63%. Voters say homelessness has worsened Homelessness produced some of the broadest agreement in the survey. 64% of California likely voters said the homelessness situation has gotten worse over the past four years. 29% said it has stayed about the same and just 7% said it has improved. More than three-quarters — 77% — supported a statewide law that would prohibit homeless tents within 500 feet of a school entrance. The proposal drew support from 69% of Democrats, 74% of independents and 91% of Republicans. Hispanic voters were nearly identical overall: 65% said homelessness has worsened, while 76% supported the proposed school-zone restriction. The two groups differed more on what they believe would be the most effective response to homelessness. Among all California voters, 23% chose mandatory drug programs and counseling, 21% selected work programs for people experiencing homelessness and 20% chose affordable housing. Among Hispanic voters, mandatory drug programs and counseling was the leading response at 34%, followed by affordable housing at 21% and work programs at 16%. Majority says rent control could help California’s housing crisis On housing, 51% of California likely voters said government-issued rent control would help solve the state’s housing crisis, while 42% said it would not and 7% were unsure. Support was highest in the San Francisco/San Jose region, where 61% said rent control would help. Sacramento/Central Valley voters were more skeptical, with 41% saying it would help and 52% saying it would not. Hispanic voters were more likely than the statewide electorate to believe rent control would help: 59% said it would, compared with 36% who said it would not. Among Hispanic Democrats, 72% said rent control would help, compared with 33% of Hispanic Republicans. Voter ID measure draws plurality support statewide The poll also asked about Proposition 39, describe as the “Voter Identification, Citizenship Verification, and Registered Voter List Administration Initiative.” Under the measure as described to respondents, in-person voters would be required to show government-issued identification, while mail voters would provide the last four digits of a designated identification used during registration. Statewide, 49% said they would vote yes, 42% no and 9% remained undecided. The regional differences were substantial. Just 34% of San Francisco/San Jose voters supported the measure, compared with 68% in San Diego. Hispanic voters expressed somewhat stronger support overall: 55% said yes, 38% no and 7% were undecided. Billionaire wealth tax leads, but many remain undecided On Proposition 40, described in the poll as a one-time 5% tax on accumulated wealth above $1 billion to fund state health care programs, 48% of California likely voters said they would vote yes, 38% said no and 14% were undecided. Hispanic voters were closely aligned with the statewide results, with 50% supporting the measure, 40% opposed and 10% undecided. Wildfire control When voters were asked which approach would be most effective in mitigating destructive wildfires, 25% statewide selected better management of power lines by utility companies and 23% chose vegetation management. Restricting development in high-fire-danger areas followed at 16%, while 13% selected planned prescribed burns. Hispanic voters ranked the same two approaches first: 27% selected better power-line management and 26% vegetation management. Iran conflict The poll also found widespread belief that the conflict with Iran is affecting the U.S. economy. Sixty-seven percent of California likely voters said it was having a “great deal” of impact, with another 16% saying it was having some impact. Among Hispanic voters, 69% said the conflict was having a great deal of impact. But only 2% named foreign policy and the Iran war as their single most important voting issue — highlighting a distinction between believing an issue affects the economy and ranking it as a top voting priority. Because some differences between the statewide and Hispanic surveys fall within or near those margins of error, comparisons are most meaningful where the gaps are larger. See the full results and breakdowns of the poll of California voters here and the poll of Hispanic voters here.

headlines.title: Couple accused of lying in wait before killing son-in-law at Dublin park
headlines.description: Prosecutors accused the in-laws of a New York Times executive of lying in wait before killing him. The Alameda County District Attorney’s Office charged 77-year-old couple Shouyong Zhang and Shili Chen with murder with a special circumstance of lying in wait and other charges in the shooting of their son-in-law, 40-year-old Jonathan McKinsey. Police say surveillance video shows both Shouyong Zhang and Shili Chen allegedly shooting McKinsey Saturday afternoon near the Dublin Sports Grounds. Witnesses helped police locate the couple and a gun was found in Chen’s possession. Police say Zhang later admitted to the shooting and told investigators a second gun found in the car was the one he allegedly used. Chen, however, invoked her Miranda rights. “While this appears to be two people that acted together, a rift between the two, and the husband made to take the blame for what the wife did,” legal analyst Steven Clark said. The allegation of lying in wait could have significant consequences if they are convicted. “The prosecution believes this was premeditated and planned, and that they waited for the victim to be in a position of vulnerability to attack him,” Clark said. Court records indicate McKinsey was in the middle of a contentious divorce and custody battle with his wife. McKinsey claimed in court filings that his wife had a history of physically assaulting him and had allowed her parents to abuse him as well. Dublin Sep 27 Dublin Sep 29 McKinsey, who was a transgender man, also alleged that his father-in-law punched him in the chest after he underwent a double mastectomy in 2010. He also claimed his mother-in-law called him a “disgusting queer” and a pervert. McKinsey’s divorce attorney, Andrea Mah, called the loss of her client a “true tragedy.” “I trust that our justice system will hold those responsible for Mr. McKinsey’s senseless death accountable,” Mah said in a statement. Court records also show McKinsey, an tech executive at The New York Times, pleaded not guilty last year to misdemeanor child abuse charges linked to accusations that he slapped one of his children and left another young child alone while he went shopping. In restraining order documents, McKinsey’s estranged wife alleged that she and her children endured years of physical, verbal and emotional abuse by McKinsey. In his own request for a restraining order, McKinsey wrote, “I am desperately afraid of what Candice will do to take revenge on me.” If convicted, Clark says both suspects could face life in prison without the possibility of parole. They are expected to be back in court Thursday morning.
headlines.source: Bob Redell, Velena Jones and Pete Suratos
